seo.title: How the regional atlas works
seo.p1: In Georgia, reptile assemblages shift with place: Colchic forests and the western coast, the Greater Caucasus high belt, and the arid basins of the east each support different species. The regional atlas turns that gradient into a practical path — pick a place on the map or in the list and see what is recorded there.
seo.p2: Each region page brings together a local species list, short habitat notes, safety context for venomous snakes, and a map. When a species catches your eye, open its full profile; when risk matters, use the venomous-snake guide.

seo.reptilesP1: Georgia sits between the Black Sea, the Greater Caucasus, and the arid east — a short geographic span that supports vipers of high mountains and Colchic forests, water snakes of rivers and wetlands, racers of dry foothills, and a widespread legless lizard often mistaken for a snake. This atlas focuses first on well-documented reptiles of Georgia, with bilingual accounts, Georgia-specific range notes, and field photography.
seo.reptilesP2: Species richness here is shaped by elevation, humidity, and refuge habitats. Western Colchic landscapes favor moisture-linked snakes such as Natrix; eastern semi-arid basins hold Macrovipera lebetina and fast colubrids; alpine and subalpine belts hold Caucasus endemics including Vipera dinniki. Counts on this page reflect published profiles in the atlas and will grow as lizards, turtles, and amphibians are added with equal rigor.
seo.venomousP1: Only a minority of Georgia’s snakes are medically significant. In this atlas, “venomous” means moderate or high risk to humans: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina), Caucasus viper (Vipera kaznakovi), Dinnik’s viper (Vipera dinniki), Transcaucasian long-nosed viper (Vipera transcaucasiana), Darevsky’s viper (Vipera darevskii), and steppe viper (Vipera renardi). Most other snakes here — grass snake, dice snake, racers, smooth snake, cat snake — are harmless to people, though several are frequently misidentified.
seo.venomousP2: Safe encounter practice is simple: do not handle wild snakes, keep distance, and learn the lookalikes common in your region. Open each profile for identification traits, habitat, and conservation status. This is educational natural-history guidance, not emergency medical advice.
seo.venomousGuideCta: Full guide: venomous snakes in Georgia
seo.regionsP1: Distribution in the atlas is recorded by Georgia’s administrative regions as a practical field layer — from Abkhazia and Adjara on the humid west to Kakheti and Kvemo Kartli in the dry east, plus the capital district of Tbilisi. A species may appear in several regions; endemics and elevational specialists are more narrowly placed.
seo.regionsP2: Use the map to move from place to fauna, then open regional pages for habitats, safety notes, and the local species list. For research-grade occurrence data, profiles also cite databases such as GBIF and the Reptile Database alongside IUCN assessments where available.

venomousSnakes.vipersBody: Six species: the Levantine viper and five Vipera. These are Georgia’s medically significant vipers.
venomousSnakes.rearFangedBody: The eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus) is listed as moderate risk. It is not a viper — the risk profile is different.
venomousSnakes.safetyTitle: What to do if you meet one
venomousSnakes.safetyLead: Most vipers will not strike unless they feel threatened. Distance and calm usually settle the encounter.
venomousSnakes.safetyDisclaimer: This page is educational and is not emergency medical instruction. If bitten, call 112.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep1Body: Never catch or move a wild snake — most bites happen during handling.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep2Body: Pass aside or back away. Even for a photo, do not close in.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep3Body: Many harmless snakes resemble vipers. Killing by mistake harms the ecosystem.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep4Body: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm and do not move the bitten arm or leg. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. This does not replace a doctor’s advice.
venomousSnakes.yardTitle: How do we get snakes out of the yard?
venomousSnakes.yardBody: Prevention near the house is a different question: shelter, food, and myths that do not work. Full practice lives in a dedicated guide.
venomousSnakes.idBody: A vertical pupil and a triangular head often point to vipers, but no rule is universal. Lookalikes have their own guide.
venomousSnakes.biteBody: Educational first steps: call 112. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet.
venomousSnakes.lookalikesTitle: Harmless species often mistaken for vipers

venomousSnakes.faqIntro: Short answers on Georgia’s venomous snakes — full detail lives on each species page.
venomousSnakes.faq1Q: How many venomous snakes are there in Georgia?
venomousSnakes.faq1A: This atlas treats six vipers as medically significant: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetinus), Transcaucasian long-nosed viper, Caucasus viper, Dinnik’s viper, Darevsky’s viper, and steppe viper. In addition, the eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus) is a moderate-risk rear-fanged species — not a viper.
venomousSnakes.faq2Q: Which venomous snake is the most dangerous?
venomousSnakes.faq2A: The Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina) is Georgia’s largest and most dangerous venomous snake; its bite can threaten human life. The Transcaucasian long-nosed viper is also high risk; the Caucasus, Dinnik’s, Darevsky’s, and steppe vipers are assessed as moderate risk.
venomousSnakes.faq3Q: Where do venomous snakes occur in Georgia?
venomousSnakes.faq3A: The Levantine viper favors dry rocky east; the Caucasus viper Colchic forests and the western coast; Dinnik’s viper the high Greater Caucasus; the Transcaucasian long-nosed viper the Meskheti–Trialeti ranges; Darevsky’s viper the Javakheti–Erusheti highlands; the steppe viper Javakheti plateaus and eastern steppes. Exact regions are on each species profile and in the regional atlas.
venomousSnakes.faq4Q: How do I tell a venomous snake from a harmless one?
venomousSnakes.faq4A: Vipers often have a vertical pupil and a more triangular head; many harmless snakes have a round pupil. The rule is not foolproof — learn species traits and habitat from the profiles instead.
venomousSnakes.faq5Q: What should I do if bitten?
venomousSnakes.faq5A: Seek medical care immediately. Stay calm, do not move the bitten arm or leg, and avoid home remedies (cutting, sucking, tourniquets). This page is educational and does not replace a clinician.

snakes.faq1Q: How many snakes are there in Georgia?
snakes.faq1A: This atlas lists snake profiles confirmed or checklist-supported for Georgia. Counts change with taxonomy and new confirmations — this page shows the current catalog.
snakes.faq2Q: Which snakes are venomous in Georgia?

snakes.faq3Q: How do I tell a viper from a harmless snake?

snakes.faq4Q: Where do snakes occur in Georgia?

snakes.faq5Q: What should I do if I meet a snake?
snakes.faq5A: Do not handle it, keep distance, and pass aside. If bitten, call 112. If a snake is in the yard or you want to reduce visits, see the practical yard guide.

lizards.faq2Q: Is the glass lizard a snake or a lizard?
lizards.faq2A: The European glass lizard (Pseudopus apodus) is a long limbless lizard, not a snake. The comparison with the slow worm and water snakes is in a dedicated guide.
lizards.faq3Q: How do I tell rock lizards apart?
lizards.faq3A: Many Darevskia species look similar. Use region, habitat, and identification traits — not colour alone.

lizards.faq5A: No — lizards in this atlas are harmless to people. Venom risk applies to certain snakes, not lizards.

snakeIdentify.metaTitle: How to tell venomous from harmless snakes in Georgia
snakeIdentify.metaDescription: Venomous vs harmless snakes in Georgia: visual cues are not universal. Giurza, Caucasian viper, water snakes, and the glass lizard — compare profiles.
snakeIdentify.keywords: venomous vs harmless snake Georgia, how to identify venomous snake, viper vs grass snake, glass lizard vs snake
snakeIdentify.title: Venomous or harmless?
snakeIdentify.subtitle: Most snakes in Georgia are harmless. A vertical pupil and a triangular head often point to vipers, but no rule is universal.
snakeIdentify.guideP1: Telling venomous from harmless by a photo is risky. A species profile is better: marks, habitat, region. This page gathers common mix-ups — not a field guarantee.
snakeIdentify.guideP2: Start with giurza and the Caucasian viper, then the other venomous species. Water snakes, the smooth snake, and the glass lizard (a lizard) are often mistaken for vipers.
snakeIdentify.signsTitle: What people look at — and why it is not enough
snakeIdentify.signsWarning: No single sign proves a snake is venomous. If you are unsure, keep your distance and compare with the atlas.
snakeIdentify.sign1Body: Vipers often have a vertical pupil; many harmless snakes have a round one. It is not always visible and it changes with light.
snakeIdentify.sign2Body: A triangular head is typical of vipers, but a harmless snake can flatten its head when threatened.
snakeIdentify.sign3Body: The grass snake can resemble the Caucasian viper; the glass lizard resembles a snake. Compare the pairs below and open the profiles.
snakeIdentify.sign4Body: Do not catch it. Do not kill it. Most are harmless. The venomous list is in a separate guide.
snakeIdentify.chainTitle: Giurza → Caucasian viper → other venomous snakes
snakeIdentify.chainBody: Start with the most dangerous, then the western forest viper, then the rest of the catalog.
snakeIdentify.pairsBody: Water snake and viper; glass lizard and snake; Montpellier snake and giurza. Each side opens a profile.
snakeIdentify.faqIntro: Short answers — the decision lives on the profile.
snakeIdentify.faq1Q: How do I tell a venomous snake from a harmless one?
snakeIdentify.faq1A: The reliable path is species identification, not a single cue. Pupil and head shape often help, but they are not universal.
snakeIdentify.faq2Q: Is the glass lizard a venomous snake?
snakeIdentify.faq2A: No. It is a legless lizard: it has eyelids and an ear opening. The profile shows how it differs from water snakes.
snakeIdentify.faq3Q: Which venomous snake should I learn first?
snakeIdentify.faq3A: Giurza (largest and most dangerous) and the Caucasian viper (west, often confused with the grass snake). Then the rest of the venomous guide.
snakeIdentify.faq4Q: Can I identify a snake from a photo with certainty?
snakeIdentify.faq4A: Often not. Use the atlas to compare, and if there is a bite — call 112. Do not wait on identification.
snakeIdentify.ctaBody: Open a species or the venomous guide. First steps after a bite are on a separate page.

snakeBite.metaDescription: Snakebite in Georgia: call 112 immediately. Stay calm and keep the bitten limb still. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. Educational page, not a medical protocol.
snakeBite.keywords: snakebite Georgia, snake bite first aid, 112 snake, what to do snake bite
snakeBite.heroImageAlt: Levantine viper in dry rocky country
snakeBite.title: Snakebite — what should you do?
snakeBite.subtitle: This page is educational and is not emergency medical instruction. If bitten, call 112.
snakeBite.disclaimerBody: Only a clinician decides treatment. This page repeats steps already published on this site’s venomous and yard guides, and it points to 112 — not folklore and not an antivenom protocol.
snakeBite.do1Body: Immediately. This is Georgia’s emergency number.
snakeBite.do2Body: Panic does not help. Wait for assistance.
snakeBite.do3Body: Keep the bitten arm or leg as still as you can until help arrives.
snakeBite.dont1Body: Cutting the wound or sucking venom does not work and causes harm.
snakeBite.dont2Body: A tourniquet is not the first-aid step described on this page.
snakeBite.dont4Body: Catching a snake for identification often causes a second bite. If you can observe safely from a distance, the atlas can help later.
snakeBite.sourcesTitle: What this page is based on
snakeBite.sourcesIntro: There is no invented medical protocol here. Only the official number and educational steps already published on this site.
snakeBite.source1Body: Georgia’s emergency number. After a bite, this is the first action.
snakeBite.source2Title: This site’s venomous guide and yard guide
snakeBite.source2Body: The same educational steps are already there: stay calm, keep the limb still, do not cut / suck / tourniquet. This page gathers them and does not add new medical advice.
snakeBite.source3Body: This is not an antivenom protocol, a toxicology manual, or a Ministry of Health guideline. If another official source is added, it will appear here.
snakeBite.speciesBody: Identification lives on the profile. After a bite, call 112 first — then, if it is safe, compare the species.
snakeBite.faqIntro: Only what is in this page’s sources.
snakeBite.faq1Q: What should I do if a snake bites me?
snakeBite.faq1A: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm and do not move the bitten arm or leg. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet.
snakeBite.faq2Q: Can I suck out the venom or cut the wound?
snakeBite.faq2A: No. This site’s guides explicitly rule that out.
snakeBite.faq3A: A bite is always an emergency for 112. Do not wait for symptoms to identify the snake.
snakeBite.faq4A: No. This is an educational page and it does not replace a clinician or 112.
snakeBite.ctaBody: Species comparison is on the profiles. Yard prevention is in a separate guide.

lizardIdentify.guideTitle: From a photo to a profile — not colour alone
lizardIdentify.guideP1: Rock lizards (Darevskia) are numerous in the Caucasus and look alike. The Caucasian agama is an agamid; the glass lizard is a legless lizard, not a snake.
lizardIdentify.guideP2: Below is a field order: photo → size → colour → range → lookalikes. The decision lives on the profile, not as a guarantee on this page.
lizardIdentify.flowBody: Each step narrows the choice. If you are unsure, open profiles and compare.
lizardIdentify.step1Body: Look at head shape, scales, limbs. A legless body may be a glass lizard or a slow worm — not necessarily a snake.
lizardIdentify.step2Body: The glass lizard is about 1–1.35 m on its profile; the slow worm is often 30–50 cm. Darevskia and the agama are smaller rock lizards. Numbers come from stats only.
lizardIdentify.step3Body: Colour is not enough for Darevskia — one species varies. Use other marks and region.
lizardIdentify.step4Body: If you know the place, open the region page. Maps for many lizards are still empty — that is a gap, not “does not occur”.
lizardIdentify.step5Body: Compare the pairs below and open the profiles. Glass lizard vs snake has its own comparison guide.
lizardIdentify.darevskiaBody: Caucasian rock lizards sit close together in appearance. Profile and region beat guessing by colour. The list below opens profiles.
lizardIdentify.featuredTitle: Agama and glass lizard stand apart
lizardIdentify.featuredBody: The agama is the only agamid in the checklist. The glass lizard is a large legless lizard — eyelids and ear openings.

lizardCompare.faqTitle: What people ask about this comparison
lizardCompare.faqIntro: Only marks confirmed on the profiles.
lizardCompare.faq1Q: Is the glass lizard a snake or a lizard?
lizardCompare.faq1A: A lizard. Unlike a snake it has movable eyelids, external ear openings, and a side fold.
lizardCompare.faq2Q: How does it differ from the slow worm?
lizardCompare.faq2A: The slow worm is smaller (often 30–50 cm) and smoother. The glass lizard is about 1–1.35 m and has a clear side fold. Both are harmless. The slow worm is a checklist candidate.
lizardCompare.faq3A: No. The profile classifies it as harmless.
lizardCompare.faq4A: Grass snakes and dice snakes are snakes often mixed up with legless lizards. They are harmless, but they are snakes.

snakesInYard.metaTitle: How to get snakes out of the yard — what works and what doesn’t
snakesInYard.metaDescription: Snakes in the yard: there is no 100% snake repellent. Reduce shelter and food so snakes do not stay. What works in Georgia — and which myths waste your time.
snakesInYard.keywords: how to get rid of snakes in the yard, snakes in yard, snake repellent, snake in garden, sulfur snake myth, milk for snakes, Georgia snakes yard
snakesInYard.heroImageAlt: A specialist safely capturing a snake in a residential yard with professional tongs
snakesInYard.title: How do we get snakes out of the yard?
snakesInYard.subtitle: There is no reliable way to “drive them out” on command. Make the yard poor for shelter and food — then a snake will not stay.
snakesInYard.whyTitle: Why do snakes enter a yard?
snakesInYard.whyLead: No method repels snakes with 100% effect. A yard usually attracts them for two reasons — shelter and food.
snakesInYard.whyShelterBody: Tall grass, shrubs, logs, stones, building materials, and wall cracks make good cover.
snakesInYard.whyFoodBody: Rodents are prey for many snakes. If mice or rats thrive in the yard, conditions improve for snakes too.
snakesInYard.coverImageAlt: A snake on rocks near rodents and tall grass — shelter and food in one place
snakesInYard.coverCaption: A yard attracts snakes when it offers shelter (rocks, logs, tall grass) and food (rodents).
snakesInYard.actionsTitle: What should we do so they stop coming in?
snakesInYard.actionsLead: The goal is not to kill or catch a snake — it is to manage the yard so neither shelter nor food remains.
snakesInYard.action1Title: Regular clearing of grass in the yard
snakesInYard.action1Body: Cut tall grass — the area becomes more open and less attractive to snakes.
snakesInYard.action2Body: Fill burrows and holes, reduce dense shrubs along edges, seal cracks in walls, and clear logs, stones, and building materials from the yard — snakes often hide there.
snakesInYard.action3Body: Rodents are food for snakes. If mice or rats are present, address that first — conditions for snakes worsen on their own.
snakesInYard.mythsLead: These methods are often recommended, but they have no reliable effect. Spend time and money on yard management instead.
snakesInYard.appearTitle: What to do if a snake is in the yard
snakesInYard.appearBody: Do not try to catch or kill it — that is dangerous and often targets a harmless species. Watch from a distance, leave an exit open, and call the right service when you need help.
snakesInYard.contactBiteBody: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm, do not move the bitten arm or leg, and avoid home remedies (cutting, sucking, tourniquets).
snakesInYard.contactAgencyBody: Call them — they can help catch the reptile safely. Do not attempt it yourself.
snakesInYard.faqIntro: Short answers — practice is above; species detail lives in the atlas.
snakesInYard.faq1Q: Is there a product that repels snakes 100%?
snakesInYard.faq1A: No. The most effective approach is reducing shelter and food. Repellent sprays, sulfur, and similar methods do not deliver reliable results. Even after yard management, one may still appear — but it will not stay.
snakesInYard.faq2Q: Why do snakes come into the yard?
snakesInYard.faq2A: Mainly for shelter and food. Tall grass, logs, stones, building materials, and rodents make a yard more attractive.
snakesInYard.faq3Q: Do milk, sulfur, or sprays work?
snakesInYard.faq3A: No — these are common myths. Yard management works better: cut grass, remove shelter, and control rodents.
snakesInYard.faq4Q: What if a snake is already in the yard?
snakesInYard.faq4A: Do not touch it or try to catch it. Watch from a distance and leave an exit. If you need the snake removed safely, call the Animal Monitoring Agency: 032 272 16 00.
snakesInYard.faq5Q: What if a snake bites someone?
snakesInYard.faq5A: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm, do not move the bitten arm or leg, and do not use home remedies (cutting, sucking, tourniquets). This page is educational and does not replace medical advice.
snakesInYard.faq6A: No. In Georgia, non-venomous species are more common and are often confused with vipers. Compare profiles in the atlas before acting out of fear.
snakesInYard.ctaTitle: Identify the species — don’t act on fear alone
snakesInYard.ctaBody: Yard management lowers risk. If you see a snake, the atlas helps with identification and a safer decision.
